items.title: pull_request_target blocked by default December 2
items.author: Allison
items.excerpt: Starting December 2, 2026, GitHub Actions will block pull_request_target events by default in all public repositories, unless an applicable Actions event policy explicitly allows them. Enforcement was previously scheduled for November 2, 2026. GitHub introduced this default rule through workflow execution protections. The rule initially runs in evaluate mode, so you can see which workflow runs it would block before enforcement begins. Private and internal repositories aren’t affected. Why we’re making this change pull_request_target runs in the context of the base repository and can access its secrets. If a workflow executes untrusted code from a fork, that code could compromise your pipeline or steal secrets. The default rule helps reduce this risk while letting you explicitly allow workflows that depend on the trigger. Brownout schedule Before permanent enforcement begins on December 2, 2026, we’ll temporarily enforce the default protection during two scheduled brownouts. These windows will help you identify affected workflows and update your policies before enforcement becomes permanent. Date Time (UTC) November 9, 2026 16:00–18:00 November 16, 2026 16:00–18:00 During each window, pull_request_target workflow attempts blocked by the default rule in affected public repositories will create failed runs with an error annotation; the workflows won’t execute. After each window, the default rule will return to evaluate mode, allowing workflows to run with warnings. Private and internal repositories aren’t affected. Prepare your workflows Before the first brownout on November 9, use Insights to see which workflow runs the rule would block. From there, you have two options: Keep the default rule in place to block pull_request_target. Explicitly allow pull_request_target in an applicable Actions event policy if your workflows depend on it. Use workflow file targeting to allow specific workflows. See how to control workflow execution to configure your policies. This change
items.why_it_matters: GitHub Actions will block pull_request_target by default in public repos from December 2. Audit open-source and client workflows now, using evaluate mode to see what would break.

items.title: Security risk assessments include repository protection status
items.author: Allison
items.excerpt: The GitHub code security risk assessment and secret risk assessment now show whether findings are in protected or unprotected repositories, helping you identify where to extend your security coverage. Organization admins and security managers can start an assessment by going to Assessments under their organization’s Security tab. This improvement is available in GitHub Enterprise Cloud and GitHub Team. It will be available for the secret risk assessment in GitHub Enterprise Server 3.24. Read more in the code security risk assessment documentation and secret risk assessment documentation. The post Security risk assessments include repository protection status appeared first on The GitHub Blog.
items.why_it_matters: GitHub security risk assessments now show whether findings are in protected or unprotected repos. A modest improvement for client security posture reviews on Team and Enterprise plans.

items.title: Building Legal Agents When You Can't See the Data - Jacob Lauritzen, CTO of Legora
items.author: Latent.Space
items.excerpt: Legora can’t read a single trace of what its agent does for a lawyer. The data belongs to the law firm’s clients. How do you build and test an agent when you can’t see its work? Jacob Lauritzen is the CTO of Legora, one of the fastest-growing companies in legal tech history. The team started in a Stockholm basement with ChatGPT, Swedish law, and a search tool. Today, a lawyer can use Legora to draft and edit Word documents, review 10,000 contracts in a single table, or run due diligence. The agent also coordinates work between lawyers, clients, and other agents. When Legora made its own acquisitions, the team used it for diligence. What we talked about • Why Legora resisted adding a model picker for years, and why it finally added one • Jacob’s estimate that models already do about 60% of legal work well, and why the rest takes a smarter model • How three engineers and three lawyers build test environments modeled on customers’ work, much like the “worlds” used in reinforcement learning • A citation problem where the model got it right 70% of the time, then 99% after one release. Legora didn’t have to change anything. • Why Legora runs everything on Azure and why it doesn’t use ElevenLabs • Tabular Review, the million-cell spreadsheet the industry copied down to the name • How intake works, how agents create lists, and how a list can start another agent • What legal engineers and forward-deployed engineers each do, and who gets to write code • The 300 Spartans slide Jacob used to argue that 20 engineers would be enough forever. Now there are 100, and he still feels short-handed. • Why Jacob finds Fable and Opus too chatty for drafting and likes Astra’s concise writing • Why drafting a long contract is a search problem • Whether model labs will cut off legal tools the way they cut off coding tools • What happens to law firm partnerships, the billable hour, and jobs for junior lawyers Legora is hiring engineers in New York, Stockholm, and London. Chapters 0:00 Cold op
items.why_it_matters: Practical look at building and evaluating LLM agents without access to production traces, directly relevant to our legal tech clients and to privacy-constrained AI feature work.

items.title: If in doubt, delete the uv.lock file
items.excerpt: I've been getting the occasional confusing Python dependency error since switching over to Python 3.15 and the rule I'm having to remember is: If in doubt, delete the uv.lock file Most of my projects are libraries which don't include a uv.lock file, since it's rude for a library dependency to lock versions for anything else that uses it. Running uv run pytest etc tends to leave uv.lock files lying around, which are listed in .gitignore and so do not get committed to my repositories. But... sometimes that uv.lock pins a version of a dependency that doesn't yet have a Python 3.15 wheel. An example from earlier today: error: Failed to build `watchfiles==1.1.1` cause: Call to `maturin.build_wheel` failed error: the configured Python interpreter version (3.15) is newer than PyO3's maximum supported version (3.14) Deleting that file and running uv run pytest again usually fixes the problem. Tags: uv, til, python
items.why_it_matters: Practical uv tip for Python 3.15 dependency errors from stale lock files, useful for our Python ML work.

items.title: The U.S. Census Bureau and “Super Intelligence”
items.excerpt: I was reminded today of AI Adoption Rate Trending Down for Large Companies, a chart produced by Apollo Global Management in September 2025, which appeared to show a slowdown in U.S. corporate AI adoption based on numbers collected by the U.S. Census Bureau. At the time I used that chart to demonstrate GPT-5 data analysis, and then to experiment with Claude's new Code Interpreter. I decided to try running those numbers again to see what had changed over the past year, and in doing so learned that the Bureau has fallen foul of Executive Order 14434, aka the asinine Super Intelligence one. First, the updated chart Every two weeks the U.S. Census Bureau runs a survey called the Business Trends and Outlook Survey (aka BTOS). Each time it goes to 200,000 businesses out of 1.2 million total - the surveyed group (a "panel") cycles such that an individual business only completes the survey every twelve weeks. The latest data is published on alternating Thursdays at 10am. I used the most recent numbers (published October 22, 2026) to create a new version (GPT-6 Astra Extra High transcript) of the AI adoption chart, updated to reflect both the last twelve months and a change that was made to the survey question sent out by the Bureau: For comparison, here's that AI adoption chart from last year (my GPT-5 version): In September 2025 the largest (250+ employees) companies answered "yes" around 12% of the time to the question about whether they used AI in "producing goods or services". Under the new "any business function" wording, by February 2026, those same large companies answered "yes" around 30% of the time, and by October 2026 that had increased to around 40%. The data in the above chart comes from the "Employment size class" XLSX file, available from here. Here's a copy of the file I used. items.title: Tiny Software Factories: Agentic Engineering DONE WRONG
items.author: IndyDevDan
items.excerpt: What's up Engineers, here's a SNEAK PEEK of the upcoming Phase 3 Agentic Engineering Course: Tiny Software Factories Phase 3 PRESALE IS LIVE (What if your agents never stopped?) https://agenticengineer.com/infinite-agentic-engineering?y=1v7ldJiyH-Y Today you'll learn agentic engineering DONE WRONG. On purpose. 🤨 You know this... You and I are the bottleneck. Every time you sit in the terminal prompting one agent back and forth, YOU are the system. Eighty percent or more of the work we're doing right now can run without us with the right system in place. In loop, you prompt. Near loop, you respond. This is blitzscaling for agentic engineering. It's not meditation, it's Xanax. It's not working out, it's a GLP-1. A useful local maximum for getting results at all costs. We stop worrying about getting things right and start getting things SHIPPED. 🏭 WHAT IS A TINY SOFTWARE FACTORY? A tiny software factory is a software factory built to solve one specific problem where a proactive agent works around the clock in a durable environment with you near the loop instead of in it. One problem. One proactive agent. Around the clock. Durable. Human near the loop, not in it. ⚠️ AGENTIC ENGINEERING DONE WRONG Tiny Software Factories is a crash course in agent anti-patterns that will NOT scale, and that's the point. The shortcuts that make a factory useful today: one agent, cron in the server, a JSON config, agent-written pages, SQLite on one box, and bash in your codebase. Each one gets you from zero to value fast. Each one breaks somewhere, and you'll know exactly where. 🚀 In this lesson, we open the empty factory: a fully built template with every feature you need and no specialization yet. Then we stack features from the feature map, ranked by value and effort: 🤖 The agent on your right: a durable agent, always on, always one message away 📋 Lists on your left: every product is a list of something. What's in your list? 🎯 Focus in the center: a generative UI where your agent builds

items.title: My AI Software Factory Ships Hundreds of PRs a Week (Here's How I Manage It)
items.author: Cole Medin
items.excerpt: My AI software factory ships hundreds of pull requests a week, and I really didn't want a control plane for it. I figured it would make things less autonomous and give me more to manage. It's turned out to be the only way I can keep up with all of it, so here's a tour of the mission control dashboard I've been building (with the factory itself doing the building!). You'll see the whole factory at a glance, the decisions that bubble up to me, how I compare versions of the factory, and what's running under the hood. It's all open source, so use it as is or just take the ideas for your own factory! ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ - Hire Viktor for your team ($100 of his work free with code COLEMEDIN100): https://ref.viktor.com/cmedin-yt Thanks to @getviktor_com for sponsoring the video! - Neon, the backend for my whole factory: https://get.neon.com/9xVbepY ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ - Join Dynamous for the new Agentic Coding Course 2.0 - the core of the course is now COMPLETE: https://dynamous.ai - AI Software Factory: https://github.com/coleam00/ai-software-factory - Mission Control dashboard: https://github.com/coleam00/factory-mission-control - Archon: https://github.com/coleam00/Archon ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ 0:00 My AI Software Factory 0:35 Mission Control at a Glance 2:10 Why It Can't Be a Dark Factory 3:20 Why I Built a Control Plane 4:17 Sponsor: Viktor 5:46 The Factory Builds Its Own Dashboard 6:31 Full Dashboard Tour 10:35 Archon Under the Hood 12:06 Neon Postgres and Functions 14:30 Live Queries with Neon Realtime 15:26 It's All Open Source! ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ Join me as I push the limits of what is possible with AI. I'll be uploading videos weekly - at least every Wednesday at 7:00 PM CDT!
